newsitem.title: USA: Fort Worth mulls bond for convention center plan.
newsitem.headline: Fort Worth mulls bond for convention center plan.

text.p: Fort Worth will consider a bond issue to finance a $42 million renovation and expansion of the city's convention center if other financing efforts fail, officials said.
City spokesman Pat Svacina said a four-member committee set up six months ago by the city and Tarrant County to study the project has so far been unable to raise the funds needed.
"We just have to come up with some financing plan. We may look at a bond issue," Svacina told Reuters.

The 30-year-old convention center brings in total annual tourism-related revenues of about $1 billion for the city and Tarrant County, but officials said it needs to be modernized soon in order to remain competitive with rival facilities.

Segi Desta, chief operating officer of the Fort Worth Convention and Visitors Bureau, said the plan includes building a 500-room hotel next to the center as well as expanding its exhibit hall and adding a ballroom and more meeting rooms.
But Texas Gov. George W. Bush recently vetoed a measure to use revenues from a state hotel bed tax to finance the plan, saying state money should not be used for local projects.
And Tarrant County, which owns the convention center but shares its direct revenues with the city of Fort Worth, has given no indication it will help finance the modernization.
The city is already planning to undertake a $100 million capital improvements bond issue in 1998, but Svacina said it could increase that amount in order to finance the convention center project.

Officials said they hope a city "crime tax" could help meet some of the cost. That tax, a half-cent sales tax increase originally levied to pay for more police officers, was approved by voters in 1993.

Diverting part of its revenues to any other project would require voters' approval. Even if it were approved, Svacina said it would generate only about $10 million for the convention center upgrade, leaving a gap of about $32 million.
